<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Forward-looking Statements</font></u></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><i><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;">IN ADDITION TO THE HISTORICAL INFORMATION, THIS ANNUAL REPORT CONTAINS CERTAIN FORWARD-LOOKING INFORMATION WITHIN THE MEANING OF SECTION&nbsp;27A OF THE SECURITIES ACT OF 1933, AS AMENDED, AND SECTION&nbsp;21E OF THE SECURITIES EXCHANGE ACT OF 1934, AS AMENDED, AND WHICH ARE SUBJECT TO THE &#147;SAFE HARBOR&#148; CREATED BY THOSE SECTIONS. THE READER OF THIS ANNUAL REPORT SHOULD UNDERSTAND THAT ALL SUCH FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS ARE SUBJECT TO VARIOUS UNCERTAINTIES AND RISKS THAT COULD AFFECT THEIR OUTCOME.&#160; THE COMPANY&#146;S ACTUAL RESULTS COULD DIFFER MATERIALLY FROM THOSE SUGGESTED BY SUCH FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS. SUCH RISKS AND UNCERTAINTIES INCLUDE, AMONG OTHERS, (1)&nbsp;COMPETITIVE PRESSURE IN THE BANKING INDUSTRY INCREASES SIGNIFICANTLY; (2)&nbsp;CHANGES IN THE INTEREST RATE ENVIRONMENT REDUCES MARGINS; (3)&nbsp;GENERAL ECONOMIC CONDITIONS, EITHER NATIONALLY OR REGIONALLY, CONTINUE TO DETERIORATE OR FAIL TO IMPROVE,&#160; RESULTING IN, AMONG OTHER THINGS, FURTHER DETERIORATION IN CREDIT QUALITY; (4)&nbsp;CHANGES IN THE REGULATORY ENVIRONMENT; (5)&nbsp;CHANGES IN BUSINESS CONDITIONS AND INFLATION; (6)&nbsp;COSTS AND EXPENSES OF COMPLYING WITH THE INTERNAL CONTROL PROVISIONS OF THE SARBANES-OXLEY ACT AND OUR DEGREE OF SUCCESS IN ACHIEVING COMPLIANCE; (7)&nbsp;CHANGES IN SECURITIES MARKETS; (8)&nbsp;FUTURE CREDIT LOSS EXPERIENCE; (9)&nbsp;CIVIL DISTURBANCES OR TERRORIST THREATS OR ACTS, OR APPREHENSION ABOUT POSSIBLE FUTURE OCCURANCES OF ACTS OF THIS TYPE; (10)&nbsp;THE INVOLVEMENT OF THE UNITED STATES IN WAR OR OTHER HOSTILITIES; AND (11) THE MATTERS DISCUSSED IN THIS REPORT UNDER &#147;ITEM 1A &#151; RISK FACTORS&#148; AND &#147;ITEM 7 &#151; MANAGEMENT&#146;S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS &#151; CRITICAL ACCOUNTING POLICIES. THEREFORE, THE INFORMATION IN THIS ANNUAL REPORT SHOULD BE CAREFULLY CONSIDERED AGAINST THESE UNCERTAINTIES AND RISKS WHEN EVALUATING THE BUSINESS PROSPECTS OF THE COMPANY.</font></i></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">PART&nbsp;1</font></u></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Item 1.&#160; Business</font></u></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">General</font></u></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Bridge Capital Holdings (the &#147;Company&#148;) is a bank holding company. The Company was incorporated in the State of California on April&nbsp;6, 2004 for the purpose of becoming the holding company for its subsidiary, Bridge Bank, National Association (the &#147;Bank&#148;). As a bank holding company, the Company is supervised by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (the &#147;FRB&#148;).</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company acquired 100% of the voting shares of the Bank effective October&nbsp;1, 2004 following approval of the Bank&#146;s shareholders on May&nbsp;20, 2004. Prior to becoming a subsidiary of the Company, the common stock of the Bank had been registered with the Comptroller of the Currency (the &#147;Comptroller&#148;) under the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934, as amended. After becoming the Bank&#146;s holding company, the Company&#146;s common stock was registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Filings by Bridge Capital Holdings are made with the SEC rather than the Comptroller and are available on the SEC&#146;s website, www.sec.gov as well as on the Company&#146;s website, www.bridgecapitalholdings.com.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank is a national banking association chartered by the Comptroller. The Bank was organized on December&nbsp;6, 2000 and commenced operations on May&nbsp;14, 2001. Its headquarters office is located at 55 Almaden Boulevard, San Jose, California, 95113. It maintains one branch office in the Silicon Valley region, and seven loan production offices located throughout the U.S.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank&#146;s lending solutions include working capital lines of credit, structured finance (asset-based lending and factoring), 7(a)&nbsp;and 504 Small Business Administration (SBA) loans, commercial real estate loans, sustainable energy project financing, growth capital loans, equipment financing, letters of credit, and corporate credit cards. The Bank&#146;s depository and corporate banking services include cash and treasury management solutions, interest-bearing term deposit accounts, checking accounts, ACH payment and wire solutions, fraud protection, remote deposit capture through its Smart Deposit Express, courier services, and online banking. Additionally, the Bank&#146;s International Banking Division serves clients operating in the global marketplace through services including foreign exchange (FX payments and hedging), letters of credit, and import/export financing. The Bank is a Preferred SBA Lender and a High Plus Delegated Authority Lender for the Export-Import Bank of the United States</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank attracts the majority of its loans and deposits from small and middle-market companies, and emerging technology companies, located throughout the San Francisco Bay Area, where it provides banking services to businesses across a variety&#160; of industries and sectors. Additionally, an increasingly larger portion of the Bank&#146;s new business acquisition comes from its national network of loan production offices. The Bank reserves the right to change its business plan at any time, and no assurance can be given that, if the Bank&#146;s proposed business plan is followed, it will prove successful.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank does not offer trust services, but it will attempt to make such services available to the Bank&#146;s customers through correspondent institutions. The deposits of the Bank are insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (the &#147;FDIC&#148;) up to applicable limits, and the Bank is a member of the Federal Reserve System.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Deposits</font></u></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank offers a wide range of deposit accounts designed to attract small and medium size commercial businesses as well as business professionals and retail customers, including a complete line of checking and savings products, such as passbook savings, &#147;Money Market Deposit&#148; accounts which require minimum balances and frequency of withdrawal limitations, NOW accounts, and bundled accounts.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Additional deposit services include a full complement of convenience oriented services, including remote deposit capture, direct payroll and social security deposit, post-paid bank-by-mail, and Internet banking, including on-line access to account information.&#160; However, at this time, the Bank does not open accounts through the Internet.&#160; Any plans to offer online account opening must be approved in advance by the Comptroller.&#160; No assurance can be given that, if applied for, such approval will be obtained.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">As the Bank has no automated teller machines, the Bank may refund all or a portion of the transaction charges incurred by its customers for their use of another bank&#146;s ATM.&#160; The majority of the Bank&#146;s deposits are obtained from businesses located in the Bank&#146;s primary service area.</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">3<a name="PB_3_174253_5335"></a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Lending Activities</font></u></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank engages in a full range of lending products designed to meet the specialized needs of its customers, including commercial lines of credit and term loans, constructions loans, and equipment loans. Additionally, the Bank extends accounts receivable, factoring and inventory financing to qualified customers.&#160; Loans are also offered through the Small Business Administration guarantee 7(a)&nbsp;and 504 loan programs (described below under &#147;Item 7. Management&#146;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations - Financial Condition and Earning Assets&#151;<i>Loan Portfolio</i>&#148;).</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank finances real estate construction projects, primarily for the construction of owner occupied and 1 to 4 unit residential developments and commercial buildings.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank directs its commercial lending principally toward businesses whose demands for credit fall within the Bank&#146;s lending limit.&#160; In the event there are customers whose commercial loan demands exceed the Bank&#146;s lending limits, the Bank seeks to arrange for such loans on a participation basis with other financial institutions.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank also extends lines of credit to individual borrowers, and provides homeowner equity loans, home improvement loans, auto financing, credit and debit cards and overdraft/cash reserve accounts.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Business Hours</font></u></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In order to attract loan and deposit business, the Bank maintains lobby hours currently between 9:00&nbsp;a.m. and 5:00&nbsp;p.m. Monday through Friday.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">For additional information concerning the Bank, see Selected Financial Data under Item 6 on page&nbsp;19.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Competition</font></u></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The commercial banking business in Santa Clara County, as it is elsewhere in California, is highly competitive, and each of the major branch banking institutions operating in California has one or more offices in the Bank&#146;s service area.&#160; The Bank competes in the marketplace for deposits and loans, principally against these banks, independent community banks, savings and loan associations, thrift and loan companies, credit unions, mortgage banking companies, and non-bank&#160; institutions such as mutual fund companies and investment brokerage firms that claim a portion of the market.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Larger banks may have a competitive advantage because of their higher lending limits and their access to relatively large marketing resources.&#160; They also perform services, such as trust services, discount brokerage and insurance services, which the Bank is not authorized or prepared to offer currently. The Bank has made arrangements with its correspondent banks and with others to provide such services for its customers.&#160; For borrowers requiring loans in excess of the Bank&#146;s legal lending limit, the Bank has offered, and intends to offer in the future, such loans on a participating basis with its correspondent banks and with other independent banks, retaining the portion of such loans which is within its lending limit.&#160; As of December&nbsp;31, 2013, the Bank&#146;s unsecured legal lending limit to a single borrower and such borrower&#146;s related parties was $26.0 million based on regulatory capital of $169.0 million.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank&#146;s business is concentrated in its service area, which primarily encompasses Santa Clara County, and also includes, to a lesser extent, the contiguous areas of Alameda, San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties.&#160; In certain lines of business the Bank has extended beyond its primary service area.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In order to compete with major financial institutions in its primary service area, the Bank uses to the fullest extent possible the flexibility that is accorded by its independent status.&#160; This includes an emphasis on specialized services, local promotional activity, and personal contacts by the Bank&#146;s officers, directors and employees.&#160; The Bank also seeks to provide special services and programs for individuals in its primary service area who are employed in the professional and business fields, such as loans for equipment, furniture, and tools of the trade or expansion of practices or businesses.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Banking is a business that depends on interest rate differentials.&#160; In general, the difference between the interest rate paid by the Bank to obtain its deposits and its other borrowings and the interest rate received by the Bank on loans extended to its customers and on securities held in the Bank&#146;s portfolio comprises the major portion of the Bank&#146;s earnings.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Commercial banks compete with savings and loan associations, credit unions, other financial institutions and other entities for funds.&#160; For instance, yields on corporate and government debt securities and other commercial paper affect the ability of commercial banks to attract and hold deposits.&#160; Commercial banks also compete for loans with savings and loan associations, credit unions, consumer finance companies, mortgage companies and other lending institutions.</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">4<a name="PB_4_174346_2897"></a></font></p>

<div>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The interest rate differentials of the Bank, and therefore its earnings, are affected not only by general economic conditions, both domestic and foreign, but also by the monetary and fiscal policies of the United States as set by statutes and as implemented by federal agencies, particularly the Federal Reserve Board.&#160; This agency can and does implement national monetary policy, such as seeking to curb inflation and combat recession, by its open market operations in United States government securities, adjustments in the amount of interest free reserves that banks and other financial institutions are required to maintain, and adjustments to the discount rates applicable to borrowing by banks from the Federal Reserve Board (FRB).&#160; These activities influence the growth of bank loans, investments and deposits and also affect interest rates charged on loans and paid on deposits.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Supervision and Regulation</font></u></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">General</font></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company and the Bank are subject to extensive regulation under both federal and state law.&#160; This regulation is intended primarily for the protection of depositors, the deposit insurance fund, and the banking system as a whole, and not the protection of shareholders of the Company.&#160; Set forth below is a summary description of some of the significant laws and regulations applicable to the Company and the Bank.&#160; The description is qualified in its entirety by reference to the applicable laws and regulations.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act</font></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On July&nbsp;21, 2010, the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (the &#147;Dodd-Frank Act&#148;) was enacted.&#160; The Dodd-Frank Act represents a fundamental restructuring of federal banking regulation.&#160; The Dodd-Frank Act is expected to have a significant impact on the Company&#146;s business operations as its provisions continue to take effect.&#160; The numerous rules&nbsp;and regulations that have been adopted and are yet to be adopted under Dodd-Frank are likely to significantly impact the Company&#146;s operations and compliance costs.&#160; Certain provisions of the Dodd-Frank Act are effective and have been fully implemented, including revisions in the deposit insurance assessment base for FDIC insurance and a permanent increase in coverage to $250,000 per account; the permissibility of paying interest on business checking accounts; the requirement that a bank holding company act as a source of financial strength for its subsidiary banks; the removal of barriers to interstate branching and required disclosure and shareholder advisory votes on executive compensation.&#160; Action in 2013 to implement the final Dodd-Frank provisions included (i)&nbsp;final new capital rules, (ii)&nbsp;a final rule&nbsp;to implement the Volcker rule&nbsp;restrictions on certain proprietary trading and investment activities and (iii)&nbsp;final rules&nbsp;and increased enforcement action by the Consumer Finance Protection Bureau.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Bank Holding Company Act</font></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company is registered as a bank holding company under the Bank Holding Company Act of 1956, as amended (the &#147;BHCA&#148;).&#160; As a bank holding company, the Company is subject to examination and supervision&#160; by the FRB and is subject to limitations on the kinds of businesses in which it can engage directly or through subsidiaries.&#160; While the Company may manage or control banks, it is generally prohibited from acquiring direct or indirect ownership or control of more than five percent of any class of voting shares of an entity engaged in non-banking activities, unless the FRB finds such activities to be &#147;so closely related to banking&#148; as to be deemed &#147;a proper incident thereto&#148; within the meaning of the BHCA.&#160; As a bank holding company, the Company may not acquire more than five percent of the voting shares of any domestic bank without the prior approval of (or, for &#147;well managed&#148; companies, prior written notice to) the FRB.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The BHCA includes minimum capital requirements for bank holding companies.&#160; See the section titled &#147;Regulation and Supervision &#151; Regulatory Capital Requirements&#148;.&#160; Under certain conditions, the FRB may conclude that certain actions of a bank holding company, such as the payment of a cash dividend, would constitute an unsafe and unsound banking practice.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Change in Bank Control</font></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The BHCA and the Change in Bank Control Act of 1978, as amended, together with regulations of the FRB and the Comptroller, require that, depending on the particular circumstances, either FRB approval must be obtained or notice must be furnished to the Comptroller and not disapproved prior to any person or company acquiring &#147;control&#148; of a company that controls a bank, such as the Company, or a national bank, such as the Bank, subject to exemptions for some transactions.&#160; Control is conclusively presumed to exist if an individual or company (i)&nbsp;acquires 25% or more of any class of voting securities of the bank or (ii)&nbsp;has the direct or indirect power to direct or cause the direction of the management and policies of the Bank, whether through ownership of voting securities, by contract or otherwise; provided that no individual will be deemed to control the bank solely on account of being director, officer or employee of the Bank.&#160; Control is presumed to exist if a person acquires 10% or more but less than 25% of any class of voting securities and either the company has registered securities under Section&nbsp;12 of the Exchange Act or no other person will own a greater percentage of that class of voting securities immediately after the transaction.</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">5<a name="PB_5_174404_3020"></a></font></p>

<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Securities Exchange Act of 1934</font></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company&#146;s common stock is registered under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended (&#147;Exchange Act&#148;). This registration requires ongoing compliance with the Exchange Act and its periodic filing requirements, as well as a wide range of federal and state securities laws. Under the Exchange Act and the SEC&#146;s rules, the Company must electronically file periodic and current reports as well as proxy statements with the SEC.&#160; The Company electronically files the following reports with the SEC: Form&nbsp;10-K (Annual Report), Form&nbsp;10-Q (Quarterly Report), Form&nbsp;8-K (Current Report), and Schedule 14A (Information Required in Proxy Statement).&#160; The Company may prepare additional filings as required.&#160; The SEC maintains an Internet site, http://www.sec.gov, at which all forms filed electronically may be accessed.&#160; Our SEC filings are also available on our website at http://www.bridgecapitalholdings.com.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Sarbanes-Oxley Act</font></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company is subject to the accounting oversight and corporate governance requirements of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, including, among other things, required executive certification of financial presentations, requirements for board audit committees and their members, and disclosure of controls and procedures and internal control over financial reporting.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Regulation of the Bank</font></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank is regulated and supervised by the Comptroller and is subject to periodic examination by the Comptroller.&#160; Deposits of the Bank&#146;s customers are insured by the FDIC up to the maximum limit of $250,000.&#160; As a national bank, the Bank is a member of the Federal Reserve System and is also subject to the regulations of the FRB.&#160; As an FDIC- insured bank, the Bank is subject to certain regulations of the FDIC.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The regulations of the Comptroller, the FDIC and the FRB govern most aspects of the Bank&#146;s business and operations, including but not limited to limiting the nature and amount of investments and loans which may be made, regulating the issuance of securities, restricting the payment of dividends and regulating bank expansion and bank activities. The Bank also is subject to the requirements and restrictions of various consumer laws and regulations.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Statutes, regulations and policies affecting the banking industry are frequently under review by Congress and by the federal bank regulatory agencies that are charged with supervisory and examination authority over banking institutions.&#160; Changes in the banking and financial services industry are likely to occur in the future.&#160; Some of the changes may create opportunities for the Bank to compete in financial markets with less regulation.&#160; However, these changes also may create new competitors in geographic and product markets which have historically been limited by law to insured depository institutions such as the Bank.&#160; Changes in the statutes, regulations, or policies that affect the Bank cannot necessarily be predicted and may have a material effect on the Bank&#146;s business and earnings.&#160; In addition, the regulatory agencies which have jurisdiction over the Bank have broad discretion in exercising their supervisory powers.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Comptroller can pursue an enforcement action against the Bank for unsafe and unsound practices in conducting its business, or for violations of any law, rule&nbsp;or regulation or provision, any consent order with any agency, any condition imposed in writing by the agency, or any written agreement with the agency.&#160; During periods of economic stress, regulatory oversight can be expected to increase and regulatory agencies become more aggressive in responding to concerns and trends identified in examinations.&#160; One result of this heightened activity is an increase in the issuance of enforcement actions.&#160; Enforcement actions may include the imposition of a conservator or receiver, cease-and-desist orders and written agreements, the termination of insurance of deposits, the imposition of civil money penalties and removal and prohibition orders against institution-affiliated parties.&#160; See &#147;Supervision and Regulation &#151; Potential Enforcement Actions and Supervisory Agreements.&#148;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In addition to the regulation and supervision outlined above, banks must be prepared for judicial scrutiny of their lending and collection practices.&#160; For example, some banks have been found liable for exercising remedies which their loan documents authorized upon the borrower&#146;s default.&#160; This has occurred in cases where the exercise of those remedies was determined to be inconsistent with the previous course of dealing between the bank and the borrower.&#160; As a result, banks must exercise caution, incur expense and face exposure to liability when dealing with delinquent loans.</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">6<a name="PB_6_174436_7748"></a></font></p>

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">
<div>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Capital Adequacy Requirements</font></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Federal regulations establish guidelines for calculating &#147;risk-adjusted&#148; capital ratios.&#160; These guidelines, which apply to banks and bank holding companies, establish a systematic approach of assigning risk weights to bank assets and commitments, making capital requirements more sensitive to differences in risk profiles among banking organizations.&#160; For these purposes, &#147;Tier 1&#148; capital consists of common equity, non-cumulative perpetual preferred stock and minority interests in the equity accounts of consolidated subsidiaries and excludes goodwill.&#160; &#147;Tier 2&#148; capital consists of cumulative perpetual preferred stock, limited-life preferred stock, mandatory convertible securities, subordinated debt and (subject to a limit of 1.25% of risk-weighted assets) general loan loss reserves.&#160; In calculating the relevant ratio, a bank&#146;s assets and off-balance sheet commitments are risk-weighted; thus, for example, generally loans are included at 100% of their book value while assets considered less risky are included at a percentage of their book value (20%, for example, for inter-bank obligations and Government Agency securities, and 0% for vault cash and U.S. Government securities).&#160; Under these regulations, to be considered adequately capitalized, banks and bank holding companies are required to maintain a risk-based capital ratio of 8%, with Tier 1 risk-based capital (primarily shareholders&#146; equity) constituting at least 50% of total qualifying capital or 4% of risk-weighted assets.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The risk-based capital ratio focuses principally on broad categories of credit risk, and may not take into account many other factors that can affect a bank&#146;s financial condition.&#160; These factors include overall interest rate risk exposure; liquidity, funding and market risks; the quality and level of earnings; concentrations of credit risk; certain risks arising from nontraditional activities; the quality of loans and investments; the effectiveness of loan and investment policies; and management&#146;s overall ability to monitor and control financial and operating risks, including the risk presented by concentrations of credit and nontraditional activities.&#160; The Comptroller has addressed many of these areas in related rule-making proposals. In addition to evaluating capital ratios, an overall assessment of capital adequacy must take account of each of these other factors including, in particular, the level and severity of problem and adversely classified assets. For this reason, the final supervisory judgment on a bank&#146;s capital adequacy may differ significantly from the conclusions that might be drawn solely from the absolute level of the bank&#146;s risk-based capital ratio.&#160; The Comptroller has stated that banks generally are expected to operate above the minimum risk-based capital ratio.&#160; Banks contemplating significant expansion plans, as well as those institutions with high or inordinate levels of risk, are required to hold capital consistent with the level and nature of the risks to which they are exposed.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Under certain circumstances, the Comptroller may determine that the capital ratios for a national bank must be maintained at levels that are higher than the minimum levels required by the guidelines.&#160; A national bank that does not achieve and maintain required capital levels may be subject to supervisory action by the Comptroller through the issuance of a capital directive to ensure the maintenance of required capital levels. \</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The federal banking agencies, including the Comptroller, have adopted regulations implementing a system of prompt corrective action under the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Improvement Act (&#147;FDICIA&#148;).&#160; The regulations establish five capital categories with the following characteristics:&#160; (1)&nbsp;&#147;Well capitalized,&#148; consisting of institutions with a total risk-based capital ratio of 10.0% or greater, a Tier&nbsp;1 risk-based capital ratio of 6.0% or greater and a leverage ratio of 5.0% or greater and which are not operating under an order, written agreement, capital directive or prompt corrective action directive; (2)&nbsp;&#147;Adequately capitalized,&#148; consisting of institutions with a total risk-based capital ratio of 8.0% or greater, a Tier&nbsp;1 risk-based capital of 4.0% or greater and a leverage ratio of 4.0% or greater and which do not meet the definition of a &#147;well capitalized&#148; institution; (3)&nbsp;&#147;Undercapitalized,&#148; consisting of institutions with a total risk-based capital ratio of less than 8.0%, a Tier&nbsp;1 risk-based capital ratio of less than 4.0%, or a leverage ratio of less than 4.0%; (4)&nbsp;&#147;Significantly undercapitalized,&#148; consisting of institutions with a total risk-based capital ratio of less than 6.0%, a Tier&nbsp;1 risk-based capital ratio of less than 3.0%, or a leverage ratio of less than 3.0%; and (5)&nbsp;&#147;Critically undercapitalized,&#148; consisting of institutions with a ratio of tangible equity to total assets that is equal to or less than 2.0%.&#160; The prompt correction action standards will change when the new Basel III capital ratios become effective.&#160; Under the new standards, in order to be considered well-capitalized, the Bank will be required to meet the new common equity Tier 1 ratio of 6.5%, an increased Tier 1 ratio of 8% (increased from 6%), a total capital ratio of 10% (unchanged) and a leverage ratio of 5% (unchanged).&#160; See &#147;&#151;Basel Accords and the New Capital Standards.&#148; The regulations establish procedures for the classification of financial institutions within the capital categories, for filing and reviewing capital restoration plans required under the regulations, and for the issuance of directives by the appropriate regulatory agency, among other matters.&#160; See &#147;Supervision and Regulation &#151; Prompt Corrective Action&#148; for additional discussion regarding regulations.</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">7<a name="PB_7_174447_141"></a></font></p>
<div style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><hr size="3" width="100%" noshade color="#010101" align="left"></div>

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">
<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">An institution that is less than well-capitalized cannot accept brokered deposits without the consent of the FDIC.&#160; The appropriate federal banking agency, after notice and an opportunity for a hearing, is authorized to treat a well capitalized, adequately capitalized or undercapitalized insured depository institution as if it had a lower capital-based classification if it is in an unsafe and unsound condition or engaging in an unsafe and unsound practice.&#160; Thus, an adequately capitalized institution can be subjected to the restrictions (described below) that are imposed on undercapitalized institutions (provided that a capital restoration plan cannot be required of the institution), and an undercapitalized institution can be subjected to the restrictions (also described below) applicable to significantly undercapitalized institutions.&#160; See &#147;Supervision and Regulation &#151; Prompt Corrective Action&#148; for additional discussion regarding federal banking agency supervision.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">At December&nbsp;31, 2013, the Company and the Bank have capital ratios that place them in the &#147;well capitalized&#148; category under the standards in effect on that date. See Note 16 to the Consolidated Financial Statements included under Item 8 of this Annual Report.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Basel Accords and the New Capital Standards</font></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The current risk-based capital guidelines that apply to the Company and the Bank are based upon the 1988 capital accord (referred to as &#147;Basel I&#148;) of the International Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (the &#147;Basel Committee&#148;), a committee of central banks and bank supervisors and regulators from the major industrialized countries.&#160; The Basel Committee develops broad policy guidelines for use by each country&#146;s supervisors in determining the supervisory policies they apply.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">A new framework and accord, referred to as Basel&nbsp;II, evolved from 2004 to 2006 out of the efforts to revise capital adequacy standards for internationally active banks. Basel&nbsp;II emphasized internal assessment of credit, market and operational risk and supervisory assessment and market discipline. The Company was not required to comply with Basel II and elected not to apply the Basel II standards.&#160; In 2010 and 2011, the Basel Committee finalized proposed reforms on capital and liquidity, generally referred to as Basel III, to further strengthen the Basel&nbsp;II framework in response to the worldwide economic downturn.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">On July&nbsp;2, 2013, the FRB and other federal banking agencies approved final rules&nbsp;implementing Basel III.&#160; The final rules&nbsp;increase the minimum requirements for both the levels and quality of capital of banking organizations, make selected changes to the calculation of risk-weighted assets and adjust prompt corrective action thresholds.&#160; The new standards, which will become effective on January&nbsp;1, 2015:</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Impose more restrictive eligibility requirements for Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Create a new minimum Tier 1 common equity ratio of 4.5%;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Increase the minimum Tier 1 capital ratio to 6.0%;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Retain the minimum total capital to risk-weighted assets ratio requirement of 8%;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Include a minimum leverage ratio of 4.0% for all banking organizations;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Create a new additional capital conservation buffer of 2.5% of risk weighted assets over each of the required capital ratios, to be phased in from 2016 to 2019, and which must be met to avoid limitations on the ability of the Bank or the Company to pay dividends, repurchase shares or pay discretionary bonuses; and</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Symbol" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&#183;</font><font size="1" style="font-size:3.0pt;">&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160;&#160; </font><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Introduce a countercyclical capital buffer of up to 2.5% during periods of excessive credit growth, as determined by the FRB.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt .5in;text-indent:-.25in;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The final rules&nbsp;also revise the prompt corrective action framework that will be effective on January&nbsp;1, 2015.&#160; Under the new prompt corrective action requirements, which are designed to complement the capital conservation buffer, insured depository institutions will be required to meet the following increased capital level requirements in order to qualify as &#147;well capitalized:&#148; (i)&nbsp;a new common equity Tier 1 capital ratio of 6.5%; (ii)&nbsp;a Tier 1 capital ratio of 8% (increased from 6%); (iii)&nbsp;a total capital ratio of 10% (unchanged from current rules); and (iv)&nbsp;a Tier 1 leverage ratio of 5% (increased from 4%).</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The final rules&nbsp;establish new qualifying criteria for regulatory capital, including new limitations on the inclusion of deferred tax assets and mortgage servicing rights.&#160; Banking organizations that had less than $15 billion in total consolidated assets as of December&nbsp;31, 2009, such as the Company, are permitted to include in Tier 1 capital trust preferred securities, subject to a limit of 25% of Tier 1 capital elements, excluding any non-qualifying capital instruments and after all regulatory capital deductions and adjustments have been applied to Tier 1 capital.&#160; The existing regulatory capital framework for 1-4 family residential mortgage exposures remains unchanged.&#160; Banking organizations with less than $250 billion in assets, such as the Company and the Bank, may make a one-time election to retain the existing treatment for most accumulated other comprehensive income, so that unrealized gains and losses on securities available for sale will not affect regulatory capital amounts and ratios.</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">8<a name="PB_8_174548_7608"></a></font></p>
<div style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><hr size="3" width="100%" noshade color="#010101" align="left"></div>
</div>
<!-- SEQ.=1,FOLIO='8',FILE='C:\JMS\C901810\14-2726-1\task6615749\2726-1-bi.htm',USER='C901810',CD='Mar 11 21:08 2014' -->

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">
<div>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company is currently evaluating the final rules&nbsp;and their expected impact on the Company, but its preliminary assessment indicates that it would meet the requirements of the final rules&nbsp;as of December&nbsp;31, 2013 if they were in effect on that date.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Deposit Insurance Coverage and Premiums</font></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Deposits at the Bank are insured by the FDIC up to applicable limits.&#160; The FDIC assesses deposit insurance premiums on each FDIC-insured institution quarterly based on annualized rates.&#160; A depository institutions&#146; FDIC insurance premium assessment rate is adjusted for risk and is based on its capital, supervisory ratings and other factors.&#160; Under FDIC regulations, the assessment base against which deposit insurance premiums are calculated is the depository institution&#146;s average total consolidated assets less the institution&#146;s average tangible equity.&#160; Assessment rates on this assessment base initially range from 5 to 35 basis points.&#160; After potential adjustment for certain risk elements, the assessments rates range from 2.5 to 45 basis points.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Dodd-Frank Act increased the minimum reserve ratio (the ratio of the net worth of the FDIC&#146;s Deposit Insurance Fund to estimated insured deposits) from 1.15% of estimated deposits to 1.35% of estimated deposits (or a comparable percentage of the asset-based assessment base described above).&#160; The Dodd-Frank Act requires the FDIC to offset the effect of the increase in the minimum reserve ratio when setting assessments for insured depository institutions with less than $10 billion in total consolidated assets, including the Bank. The FDIC has until September&nbsp;30, 2020 to achieve the new minimum reserve ratio of 1.35%.&#160; FDIC insured institutions are required to pay a Financing Corporation assessment, in order to fund the interest on bonds issued to resolve thrift failures in the 1980s. For the quarterly period ended December&nbsp;31, 2009, the Financing Corporation assessment equaled 1.02 basis points for each $100 in domestic deposits.&#160; These assessments, which may be revised based upon the level of deposits, will continue until the bonds mature in the years 2017 through 2019.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The FDIC may terminate the deposit insurance of any insured depository institution, including the Bank, if it determines after a hearing that the institution has engaged in unsafe or unsound practices, is in an unsafe or unsound condition to continue operations or has violated any applicable law, regulation, rule, order or condition imposed by the FDIC.&#160; It also may suspend deposit insurance temporarily during the hearing process for the permanent termination of insurance, if the institution has no tangible capital.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Prompt Corrective Action</font></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The federal banking agencies, including the Comptroller, have adopted regulations implementing a system of prompt corrective action under FDICIA.&#160; The regulations establish five capital categories:&#160; (1)&nbsp;&#147;well capitalized,&#148;; (2)&nbsp;&#147;adequately capitalized,&#148;; (3) &#147;undercapitalized,&#148;; (4) &#147;significantly undercapitalized,&#148;; and (5)&nbsp;&#147;critically undercapitalized,&#148;&#160; See &#147;Capital Adequacy Requirements&#148; above for a discussion of the features of each capital category.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The FDIC has authority: (a)&nbsp;to request that an institution&#146;s primary regulatory agency (in the case of the Bank, the Comptroller) take enforcement action against it based upon an examination by the FDIC or the agency, (b)&nbsp;if no action is taken within 60 days and the FDIC determines that the institution is in an unsafe and unsound condition or that failure to take the action will result in continuance of unsafe and unsound practices, to order that action be taken against the institution, and (c)&nbsp;to exercise this enforcement authority under &#147;exigent circumstances&#148; merely upon notification to the institution&#146;s primary regulatory agency.&#160; This authority gives the FDIC the same enforcement powers with respect to any institution and its subsidiaries and affiliates as the primary regulatory agency has with respect to those entities.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">An undercapitalized institution is required to submit an acceptable capital restoration plan to its primary federal bank regulatory agency.&#160; The banking agency may not accept a capital restoration plan unless the agency determines, among other things, that the plan &#147;is based on realistic assumptions, and is likely to succeed in restoring the institution&#146;s capital&#148; and &#147;would not appreciably increase the risk&nbsp;.&nbsp;.&nbsp;. to which the institution is exposed.&#148;</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">9<a name="PB_9_174609_8146"></a></font></p>
<div style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><hr size="3" width="100%" noshade color="#010101" align="left"></div>
</div>
<!-- SEQ.=1,FOLIO='9',FILE='C:\JMS\C901810\14-2726-1\task6615749\2726-1-bi.htm',USER='C901810',CD='Mar 11 21:08 2014' -->

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">
<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">FDICIA provides that the appropriate federal regulatory agency must require an insured depository institution that is significantly undercapitalized, or that&nbsp;is undercapitalized and either fails to submit an acceptable capital restoration plan within the time period allowed by regulation or fails in any material respect to implement a capital restoration plan accepted by the appropriate federal banking agency, to take one or more of the following actions:&#160; (a)&nbsp;sell enough shares, including voting shares, to become adequately capitalized; (b)&nbsp;merge with (or be sold to) another institution (or holding company), but only if grounds exist for appointing a conservator or receiver; (c)&nbsp;restrict specified transactions with banking affiliates as if the &#147;sister bank&#148; exception to the requirements of Section&nbsp;23A of the Federal Reserve Act did not exist; (d)&nbsp;otherwise restrict transactions with bank or non-bank affiliates; (e)&nbsp;restrict interest rates that the institution pays on deposits to &#147;prevailing rates&#148; in the institution&#146;s &#147;region&#148;; (f)&nbsp;restrict asset growth or reduce total assets; (g)&nbsp;alter, reduce or terminate activities; (h)&nbsp;hold a new election of directors; (i)&nbsp;dismiss any director or senior executive officer who held office for more than 180&nbsp;days immediately before the institution became undercapitalized, provided that in requiring dismissal of a director or senior executive officer, the agency must comply with procedural requirements, including the opportunity for an appeal in which the director or officer will have the burden of proving his or her value to the institution; (j)&nbsp;employ &#147;qualified&#148; senior executive officers; (k)&nbsp;cease accepting deposits from correspondent depository institutions; (l)&nbsp;divest non-depository affiliates which pose a danger to the institution; (m)&nbsp;be divested by a parent holding company; and (n)&nbsp;take any other action which the agency determines would better carry out the purposes of the prompt corrective action provisions.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In addition to the foregoing sanctions, without the prior approval of the appropriate federal banking agency, a significantly undercapitalized institution may not pay any bonus to any senior executive officer or increase the rate of compensation for a senior executive officer without regulatory approval.&#160; If an undercapitalized institution has failed to submit or implement an acceptable capital restoration plan the appropriate federal banking agency is not permitted to approve the payment of a bonus to a senior executive officer.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Not later than 90&nbsp;days after an institution becomes critically undercapitalized, the institution&#146;s primary federal bank regulatory agency must appoint a receiver or a conservator, unless the agency, with the concurrence of the FDIC, determines that the purposes of the prompt corrective action provisions would be better served by another course of action.&#160; Any alternative determination must be documented by the agency and reassessed on a periodic basis.&#160; Notwithstanding the foregoing, a receiver must be appointed after 270&nbsp;days unless the FDIC determines that the institution has positive net worth, is in compliance with a capital plan, is profitable or has a sustainable upward trend in earnings, and is reducing its ratio of non-performing loans to total loans, and unless the head of the appropriate federal banking agency and the chairperson of the FDIC certify that the institution is viable and not expected to fail.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The FDIC is required, by regulation or order, to restrict the activities of critically undercapitalized institutions.&#160; The restrictions must include prohibitions on the institution&#146;s doing any of the following without prior FDIC approval:&#160; entering into any material transactions not in the usual course of business, extending credit for any highly leveraged transaction; engaging in any &#147;covered transaction&#148; (as defined in Section&nbsp;23A of the Federal Reserve Act) with an affiliate; paying &#147;excessive compensation or bonuses&#148;; and paying interest on &#147;new or renewed liabilities&#148; that would increase the institution&#146;s average cost of funds to a level significantly exceeding prevailing rates in the market.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Potential Enforcement Actions and Supervisory Agreements</font></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Under federal law, national banks, their holding companies and their respective institution-affiliated parties may be the subject of potential enforcement actions by the Comptroller or the FRB for unsafe and unsound practices in conducting their businesses, or for violations of any law, rule&nbsp;or regulation or provision, any consent order with any agency, any condition imposed in writing by the agency or any written agreement with the agency.&#160; During periods of economic stress, regulatory oversight can be expected to increase and regulatory agencies become more aggressive in responding to concerns and trends identified in examinations.&#160; One result of this heightened activity is an increase in the issuance of enforcement actions.&#160; Enforcement actions may include the imposition of a conservator or receiver, cease-and-desist orders and written agreements, the termination of insurance of deposits, the imposition of civil money penalties and removal and prohibition orders against institution-affiliated parties.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Payment of Dividends</font></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Company</font></u><i><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;"> &#151; </font></i><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Historically, the Company has not paid dividends but has retained earnings to support growth.&#160; The ability of the Company to make dividend payments is subject to statutory and regulatory restrictions.&#160; Under California law, a California corporation such as the Company may make a distribution to its shareholders if the corporation&#146;s retained earnings equal at least the amount of the proposed distribution.&#160; In the event sufficient retained earnings are not available for the proposed distribution, a California corporation may nevertheless make a distribution to its shareholders if, giving effect to the distribution, the value of the corporation&#146;s assets would equal or exceed the value of its liabilities plus the amount of shareholder preferences, if any. It is the FRB&#146;s policy that bank holding companies should generally pay dividends on common stock only out of income available over the past year, and only if prospective earnings retention is consistent with the organization&#146;s expected future needs and financial condition.</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">10<a name="PB_10_174645_7091"></a></font></p>

<br clear="all" style="page-break-before:always;">
<div style="font-family:Times New Roman;">
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The primary source of funds for payment of any dividends by the Company to its shareholders will be the receipt of dividends and management fees from the Bank.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><u><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Bank</font></u><i><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-style:italic;"> - </font></i><font size="2" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Board of Directors of a national bank may declare the payment of dividends depending upon the earnings, financial condition and cash needs of the bank and general business conditions.&#160; A national bank may not pay dividends from its capital.&#160; All dividends must be paid out of net profits then on hand, after deducting losses and bad debts.&#160; The approval of the Comptroller is required for the payment of dividends if the total of all dividends declared by the bank in any calendar year would exceed the total of its net profits of that year combined with its retained net profits of the two preceding years, less any required transfers to surplus or a fund for the retirement of any preferred stock.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">In addition to the above requirements, guidelines adopted by the Comptroller set forth factors which are to be considered by a national bank in determining the payment of dividends.&#160; A national bank, in assessing the payment of dividends, is to evaluate the bank&#146;s capital position, its maintenance of an adequate allowance for loan and lease losses, and the need to revise or develop a comprehensive capital plan.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">The Comptroller also has broad authority to prohibit a national bank from engaging in banking practices which it considers to be unsafe or unsound.&#160; It is possible, depending upon the financial condition of the national bank in question and other factors, that the Comptroller may assert that the payment of dividends or other payments by a bank is considered an unsafe or unsound banking practice and therefore, implement corrective action to address such a practice.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Accordingly, the future payment of cash dividends by the Company will not only depend upon the Bank&#146;s earnings during any fiscal period but will also depend upon the assessment of its Board of Directors of capital requirements and other factors, including dividend guidelines and the maintenance of an adequate allowance for loan and lease losses.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Community Reinvestment Act</font></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Pursuant to the Community Reinvestment Act (the &#147;CRA&#148;) of 1977, the federal regulatory agencies that oversee the banking industry are required to use their authority to encourage financial institutions to help meet the credit needs of the local communities in which such institutions are chartered, consistent with safe and sound banking practices.&#160; When conducting an examination of a financial institution such as the Bank, the agencies assess the institution&#146;s record of meeting the credit needs of its entire community, including low- and moderate- income neighborhoods.&#160; This record is taken into account in an agency&#146;s evaluation of an application for creation or relocation of domestic branches or for merger with another institution.&#160; Failure to address the credit needs of a bank&#146;s community may also result in the imposition of certain other regulatory sanctions, including a requirement that corrective action be taken.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Transactions with Affiliates</font></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Sections&nbsp;23A and&nbsp;23B of the Federal Reserve Act and the FRB&#146;s Regulation&nbsp;W limit transactions between a bank and its affiliates and limit a bank&#146;s ability to transfer to its affiliates the benefits arising from the bank&#146;s access to insured deposits, the payment system and the discount window and other benefits of the Federal Reserve system.&nbsp; The statute and regulation impose quantitative and qualitative limits on the ability of a bank to extend credit to, or engage in certain other transactions with, an affiliate (and a non-affiliate if an affiliate benefits from the transaction).&nbsp; However, certain transactions that generally do not expose a bank to undue risk or abuse the safety net are exempted from coverage under Regulation&nbsp;W.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><b><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;font-weight:bold;">Tying Arrangements and Transactions with Affiliated Persons</font></b></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">A bank is prohibited from tie-in arrangements in connection with any extension of credit, sale or lease of property or furnishing of services.&#160; For example, with some exceptions, a bank may not condition an extension of credit on a promise by its customer to obtain other services provided by it, its holding company or other subsidiaries (if any), or on a promise by its customer not to obtain other services from a competitor.</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">Directors, officers and principal shareholders of the Bank, and the companies with which they are associated, may have banking transactions with the Bank in the ordinary course of business.&#160; Any loans and commitments to loan included in these transactions must be made in compliance with the requirements of applicable law, on substantially the same terms, including interest rates and collateral, as those prevailing at the time for comparable transactions with other persons of similar creditworthiness, and on terms not involving more than the normal risk of collectability or presenting other unfavorable features.</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p align="center" style="margin:0in 0in .0001pt;text-align:center;"><font size="2" face="Times New Roman" style="font-size:10.0pt;">11<a name="PB_11_174702_455"></a></font></p>
